Abandoned Train Towns

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Abandoned railway towns tell the story of colonial and economic conquest, and the failure to embrace and maintain vital transport routes.

Unique Selling Point:
The South African rail network is an historical map of colonial conquest. In the late 1800s, as mining developed in the interior, rail lines were built connecting the mines to the ports, and steam trains criss-crossed the vast South Africa landscape. They played a vital role in the South African (Anglo-Boer) War, and bridges built in the 1800s are still standing. By 1912 when the Union Government was formed, the four rail networks were amalgamated and taken over by the government, becoming a powerful economic and political tool.
In 1924 after the industrial Depression, the white – “European” - minority enjoyed the first affirmative action appointments - unskilled white labour was actively recruited onto the railways to ensure they did not sink below the level of the “non-European” workers, and black rail employee numbers were eclipsed by white workers. Entire towns were developed around the railways, providing a vast network of solidly built brick houses and recreational facilities for white employees, with crude rondavels provided for migrant black workers. The South African Railways and Harbours, SAR&H, ran these towns, with the station masters playing the role of mayor, and the railway police keeping people in their place.
The SAR&H built tracks deep into the farming areas, providing sidings for farmers to leave their milk for collection, collect their post, and deliver their produce to market. It ensured political patronage, but over time this vast network became uneconomical. Coal was cheap, and with a ready supply of white artisans and labour, South Africa kept steam trains running for far longer than the rest of the world. But when railway workers’ kids left and got University degrees, the white train drivers refused to have black stokers and train assistants in their cabs, Steam began to die and diesel engines took over.
The uneconomical routes were gradually abandoned and entire towns began to die - Klipplaat and Touws River are prime examples, both were substantial depots and railway towns in their heyday. Today they are sad, falling-apart towns, the majority of adult residents dependent on SASSA grants, with the few available jobs provided by the municipality and surrounding farms.


Summary:
Every station and rail siding leading to these towns has been abandoned, vandalised, and scrap dealers have fed off them like vultures. This vast infrastructure and state asset was simply abandoned as senior Transnet officials began to run and own lucrative trucking companies. Indecision and lack of leadership in the protection of assets has resulted in every railway station either destroyed or occupied by farm workers.
Transnet’s lack of vision or any clear policy of transferring ownership has resulted in buildings either being burnt for insurance claims or simply destroyed as an act of defiance. Today people in these forgotten towns equate the failed Transnet with the failures of the ANC, and the overloaded, crumbling highways are dominated by lucrative trucking companies, often owned by politicians.
But in fact, the railways began to fade and abandon both their employees and their infrastructure in the mid-1980s under the Nationalist Government.
We will tell this history through two towns. Klipplaat and Touws River, with two main characters in each town. Willie Marais was a stream train driver born directly opposite the station in Touws River, which was built in 1881. His father was a “poor white” who never managed to own his own home. Willie grew up with the benefits of a good high school, now vandalised and abandoned, and recreational facilities provided for the white workers, with movies on Saturday night in the railway hall, and security ensured by the railway police.
In 1992 he was retrenched. He spent the next 20 years working as an undertaker across the country. He has returned to Touws River to restore the home he grew up in, with dreams of also restoring the demolished station to its former glory. It was burnt for an alleged insurance payout, and taken apart brick by brick, one roof sheet at a time. Willie manged to save two of the verandah pillars which were built from ships’ masts in the 1800s.
Louis Langeveld is an elder of Klipplaat, now retired. He was the headmaster of Klipplaat High. His father worked for the railways and his childhood is richly populated with memories of a thriving railway town. His father witnessed the royal visit of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth together with their daughters Elizabeth and Margaret in 1947 when the train stopped in Klipplaat to take on coal and water. The station master hosted them for a meal at the station in its once-grand wooded dining hall.
Louis used to fetch the Saturday night films from the train and snuck into the projection room, hiding from the station master and his railway police lackeys – he was not allowed in the hall as he is coloured. In 1986 when economic sanctions began to bite, SAR&H employees were offered retrenchment packages or transfers to bigger depots. The town’s demographic in 1986 was 2,500 whites, 2,000 coloured inhabitants and roughly 1,000 black Africans.
Today only two white people remain, Johan and his wife Chantel Loggerenberg, they own and run the former Railway Hotel, now the Hotel Charles, and the rest of the population of 13,000 are either living in shacks or in the railway houses. Johan van Loggerenberg is a secondary character in the Klipplaat story. He was born in Klipplaat, and went to the junior schools and the middle school in town. He lived in one of the “white” railway houses built in the 1940s. His father worked as a rail assistant until he was retrenched. As the railway workers left one by one, the shops began to close and slowly the coloured people began to buy up the old railway houses built for the whites. Now the four taverns and three shops are owned by Ethiopian and Somalian shopkeepers. People survive off SASSA grants and the few jobs provided by the Municipality.





Further information:
The people of Klipplaat are bitter about being abandoned by Transnet and every SAR&H building that was not occupied has been systematically destroyed. The only remnant of the heyday of this railway town is a sad, heavily graffitied steam engine.
Enroute to Gqeberha, there are many abandoned sidings - Mount Stewart has the most beautiful old Methodist church, and a trading store built by the Cawood clan. Rich in settler history, the Cawood clan farmed here for generations and the trading store still operated until a few years back. Today, Richelle and David Olifant live in the station master’s house. They are farm workers, and remember trains passing in 2018.
At Baroe siding, the station houses are inhabited by Shane Martins and Joane van Wyk. Three years and one month ago they visited the Transnet offices in Uitenhage to get permission to live in the houses - they are still waiting for the contract. They moved here off the farms to be closer to transport. In 2020 the last train went past carrying stones from a quarry down the line to Gqeberha.

Script:


Opening sequence - drone tracking railway line and lifting, revealing Karoo Music and sounds of trains on a faint reverb echo
Script: 22,000 km of track
connecting the most remote corners of the country -
an economic boom on the back of colonial conquest.
Today, endless trucks thunder down crumbling roads…
past derelict railway towns, whose residents have grown weary of the promises of change.
Upsound of travelling
CLIP 0023 LINK CLIP So we are on our way to Touws River, once a proud railway town. But now not so much, we are going to see what's become of it, mostly because of this right here - trucks on the road
Upsounds
Script A steam locomotive at the town’s entrance is a reminder of a different time in this corner of the Western Cape. A time Willie Marais remembers well.
Govan: How does it feel to be in the train
Willie No, my thoughts go far back to when I began
Govan. Uncle drove steam, diesel and the electric trains- what the best in your opinion
Willie “ Steam. …….
Govan” Because it shakes you so much
Willie. No, not just because of that but because it feels like you are really working, because everything is physical you work with your hands. Diesel, you sit there and all you do is make the driver tea, that’s the hardest you work. ….but here you work physically and you keep the engine going.
Script: Willie’s father - a railway worker - had big dreams for his son: that he would one day be a train driver.
Willie: I was born in Touws River in front of the station, my first view of life was of the station.
Script: When Willie was born, 60% of white Afrikaners either worked on the railways, or had relatives dependent on a fully functioning railway
Upsounds of steam trains
Script: Touws River thrived around the large depot, servicing locomotives before they crossed the mountains into the Great Karoo. The Railways built houses and other facilities, and the station master was the de facto mayor.
GOVAN : let’s look at the station
Willie “There is nothing left here , it’s a ruin- in the early years it was a hotel.This was the waiting room and the kitchen was at the back
Script. Accidently set alight in 2012 – what remained was systematically plundered.
Govan: Did Uncle manage to save anything?
Willie 00:01:57:02 Yes, the pillars that stood there in front, there were two and the two that remained I saved for PRASA in case if they restore the building because they were from the old days made from ship masts from 1700
Script: It’s a pattern repeated across the country.
But, the assumption that the collapse and plunder, are entirely the fault of state capture, is incorrect. The demise of most railway towns like Touwsriver, began in the mid 80’s. It was a time when railway accountants took a red pen to anything considered uneconomical. District lines were cut off and 400 passenger routes shut down.
LINK Try to picture it - 40 passenger trains stopping at this station every single day, now you will be lucky to see two freight carriages passing through.
Script: The Touwsriver depot was deemed uneconomical and overnight 1000’s of people lost their jobs – the life blood seeped away and the town was stranded.
Willie 00:04:42:23 When the Railways closed in Touws River the heartbeat died because all the people were gone.
Script: Out of work Willie left Touwsiver and became an undertaker for the next 30 years
BREAK
Links: “ This is Touws Rivers new station, without the trains this railway town's focus has turned to the highway.
SCRIPT: Now 80% of freight is carried by trucks. Many of our roads are disintegrating and deadly accidents are all too common.
CRASH
Script: How did we get to this point? Since 1931, the state enjoyed a monopoly and most freight went by rail. Journalist and train enthusiast Paul Ash tells us that the fate of our trains was sealed in the late 70’s
Paul Ash “Act 14 of the Transportation Act basically opened a loophole for .. truck operators to operate permit free within 80km of their headquarters. The trucking companies just exploited that loophole by building garages ….160km apart, 00:02:28:05 …leading to the freefall we have today.
(Back to Govan in the car travelling )
Script: As we hit the road again we pass a broken freight train and it reminds me of what a jealous god Transnet is- will they ever grant private concessions spoken about for the last 12 years.
Paul Transnet realizes that it's going to have to let go of some of its so-called crown jewels and let private operators do what they are unable or unwilling to do.
Script: Matjiesfonetin just 40 km north of Tousriver is a great example of what’s possible - a perfectly preserved railway town, dating back to the 1800’s, and despite Transnet still owning the station, its tourism and private business keeping this town alive
LINK: Clip 255 this is what the Touwsriver station would have looked like, there is your real sense of the history, Matjiesfontein shows how the station can keep the towns economy running, even when there aren’t that many trains coming in
Break road trip shots
Script: Heading to the Eastern Cape we follow a former district line , from Gquberha to Graaf Reniet, once a major freight route cut off 30 years ago. Surprisingly Transnet appeared to be reviving this branch investing millions repairing the line.
Link: We are on the road to Klipplaat, it used to be a significant railway junction and depot. …the interesting thing between Kariega and Klipplaat along the railway line are all these small little towns, really just stations, …. but for all intents and purposes its dead
BREAK
SCRIPT: Dead they might be, but they’re also full of history
Roadtrip with church
Tim day 1 Clip 122 Link; This is Mount Stewart, when these tracks were laid in the late 1800s it gave the wool and produce farmers access to the international markets and this trading store became the heart of the farming community
Pause
Tim Day 1Clip 132 The railway and this trading store transformed Mount Stewart, the farmers built homes they built a church and established a community but now …..there is only a handful of people living here
BREATH with establishers of Klipplaat
LINK 230 you know Klipplaat was once a thriving railway junction a cross roads for trains from around the country, now it’s just a bleak town at the end of the road
BREATH

Script: Louis Langeveld, is a retired headmaster and son of a railway worker. He’s fighting to keep Klipplaat on the map and provide hope for those left behind
Tim Day 2 Clip0276 00:01:05:06 Govan: What's probably the most vivid image you have of your childhood
00:03:50:06 - Louis: When we played rugby against other schools, …… there was a train called the Polkey. And when we played, that Polkey was shunting up and down. But every time when you see us playing, …….when they pull the siren. All the other kids that doesn't know trains stopped. And they looked at the train and so we scored
Script: Now it’s the poorest town in this district, anyone who could find work elsewhere left – unemployment and poverty stalk this place
Tim Day 2 Clip0276 00:22:33:25 - Louis: It's hard to see kids from 8, 10 years buying …..Tik. 0:22:56:13 this is a big problem in Klipplaat, drugs and teenage pregnancy.
Script: This is its main street - the shops and banks long closed. Bad news in a town without so much- as an ATM.
Break
Johan 00:12:06:15 - We had our own rugby team, there was every Saturday evening, Saturday there was rugby here, there wasn't a parking space in front of the hotel. The Recreation centre up the road we had dances, there was a cinema, there was everything, everything was here.
Script: Now, says Johan van Loggerenberg, it’s almost impossible to get a taxi to the nearest big town.
He’s the son of a railway worker, born in this house opposite the station.
Johan There was a bridge here where you could walk to the station, and there was a platform, a neat platform, there were fish ponds here. Yes rose beds, everything
Clip 179 00:01:56:11Govan: Fish Ponds!
When did the station get so destroyed
00:02:03:18 -Johan:It was after they closed down here in 1990 1991; it was just systematically dismantled
Govan: Now there's almost nothing left. die dak is weg, die duur is weg, die vensters
Script: It’s a town left stripped and plundered by locals and passing scrap dealers.
Now, less of a railway town than a SASSA town, people here survive on state grants, monthly pensions of around 2080 rand, and COVID unemployment grants of 350 rand.
Govan: Are you angry at Transnet for leaving?
Louis: Govan to be honest, we all were angry because they left without informing the community or without handing over the assets to the community - I'm sad to see the town and state that this now. One of the saddest moment was when the RI the recreational hall was set alight one evening and we were cross because it was the only facility, the only hall we could use for functions like school activities, concerts, weddings and 21st birthdays and things like.
SCRIPT: Johan has owned the former railway hotel, once popular with hunters, for 14 years. But, the game moved away during the drought, and now the rooms stand empty.
But somehow everyone clings to hope that the trains will run once again …. and life will come back

Johan: So a guy must just be brave and be positive, but for how long.
I will hope and pray that things will be like they used to be
00:00:16:19 - Govan: Will you ever leave Klipplaat?
00:00:25:12 Johan: Oh, I don't know, I'll probably end up dying here..

LINK Clip 385 The people in these towns are defiant, they refuse to believe their towns are dying, but the truth is they are desperate for a miracle, and it just doesn’t look like the trains will ever roll back in
Clip0276 00:23:31:18 -Louis: , I'm not going to leave Klipplaat. …I am I'm going to fight for this community
Script: Willie's heart belongs in Touwsriver- his daughter is buried in the graveyard and his father's home awaits him. He dreams of restoring the station and that the trains will stop here - once more.

After spending time with him, and the other people we met on our journey, I hope he's right."

Tuesday Promo. 21 seconds Tim Day 2 Clip 239 Tracks have been ripped out and stations stripped bare. But the fate of these railway towns was sealed decades ago
Adam day 1 Clip0071 Willie 00:04:42:23 When the Railways closed in Touws River the heartbeat died because all the people were gone.
Tim Day 2 Clip 245 South Africa’s railway towns are dying but the people who have been left behind cling onto hope

21 Second Promo 1: Railway towns across the country cling onto hope
Clip0276 00:23:31:18 -Louis: , I'm not going to leave Klipplaat. …I am going to do for Klipplaat what I can do, I'm going to fight for this community
Script: But the last trains passed this way years ago and the station stripped bare

21 sec Promo 2: VO: These small towns in the Eastern Cape once thrived off the busy railways…
Johan 00:12:06:15 - We had our own rugby team, there was every Saturday evening, Saturday there was rugby here, there wasn't a parking space in front of the hotel. The Recreation centre up the road we had dances, there was a cinema, there was everything, everything was here.
VO: Now, trucks thunder down broken highways, leaving THEM in their dust…


Promo 3 21sec :

VO: Born opposite the railway station in Touws River, fulfilling his fathers dream to be a train driver, WILLIE Marais longs for those days when life was simple.
Adam day 1 Clip 44 Willie. it feels like you are really working, because everything is physical you work with your hands. Diesel, you sit there and all you do is make the driver tea, that’s the hardest you work. ….but here you work physically and you keep the engine going

reverb echo Script: 22,000 km of track connecting the most remote corners of the country - an economic boom on the back of colonial conquest. Today, endless trucks thunder down crumbling roads… past derelict railway towns, whose residents have grown weary of the promises of change. Upsound of travelling CLIP 0023 LINK CLIP So we are on our way to Touws River, once a proud railway town. But now not so much, we are going to see what's become of it, mostly because of this right here - trucks on the road Upsounds Script A steam locomotive at the town’s entrance is a reminder of a different time in this corner of the Western Cape. A time Willie Marais remembers well. Govan: How does it feel to be in the train Willie No, my thoughts go far back to when I began Govan. Uncle drove steam, diesel and the electric trains- what the best in your opinion Willie “ Steam. ……. Govan” Because it shakes you so much Willie. No, not just because of that but because it feels like you are really working, because everything is physical you work with your hands. Diesel, you sit there and all you do is make the driver tea, that’s the hardest you work. ….but here you work physically and you keep the engine going. Script: Willie’s father - a railway worker - had big dreams for his son: that he would one day be a train driver. Willie: I was born in Touws River in front of the station, my first view of life was of the station. Script: When Willie was born, 60% of white Afrikaners either worked on the railways, or had relatives dependent on a fully functioning railway Upsounds of steam trains Script: Touws River thrived around the large depot, servicing locomotives before they crossed the mountains into the Great Karoo. The Railways built houses and other facilities, and the station master was the de facto mayor. GOVAN : let’s look at the station Willie “There is nothing left here , it’s a ruin- in the early years it was a hotel.This was the waiting room and the kitchen was at the back Script. Accidently set alight in 2012 – what remained was systematically plundered. Govan: Did Uncle manage to save anything? Willie 00:01:57:02 Yes, the pillars that stood there in front, there were two and the two that remained I saved for PRASA in case if they restore the building because they were from the old days made from ship masts from 1700 Script: It’s a pattern repeated across the country. But, the assumption that the collapse and plunder, are entirely the fault of state capture, is incorrect. The demise of most railway towns like Touwsriver, began in the mid 80’s. It was a time when railway accountants took a red pen to anything considered uneconomical. District lines were cut off and 400 passenger routes shut down. LINK Try to picture it - 40 passenger trains stopping at this station every single day, now you will be lucky to see two freight carriages passing through. Script: The Touwsriver depot was deemed uneconomical and overnight 1000’s of people lost their jobs – the life blood seeped away and the town was stranded. Willie 00:04:42:23 When the Railways closed in Touws River the heartbeat died because all the people were gone. Script: Out of work Willie left Touwsiver and became an undertaker for the next 30 years BREAK Links: “ This is Touws Rivers new station, without the trains this railway town's focus has turned to the highway. SCRIPT: Now 80% of freight is carried by trucks. Many of our roads are disintegrating and deadly accidents are all too common. CRASH Script: How did we get to this point? Since 1931, the state enjoyed a monopoly and most freight went by rail. Journalist and train enthusiast Paul Ash tells us that the fate of our trains was sealed in the late 70’s Paul Ash “Act 14 of the Transportation Act basically opened a loophole for .. truck operators to operate permit free within 80km of their headquarters. The trucking companies just exploited that loophole by building garages ….160km apart, 00:02:28:05 …leading to the freefall we have today. (Back to Govan in the car travelling ) Script: As we hit the road again we pass a broken freight train and it reminds me of what a jealous god Transnet is- will they ever grant private concessions spoken about for the last 12 years. Paul Transnet realizes that it's going to have to let go of some of its so-called crown jewels and let private operators do what they are unable or unwilling to do. Script: Matjiesfonetin just 40 km north of Tousriver is a great example of what’s possible - a perfectly preserved railway town, dating back to the 1800’s, and despite Transnet still owning the station, its tourism and private business keeping this town alive LINK: Clip 255 this is what the Touwsriver station would have looked like, there is your real sense of the history, Matjiesfontein shows how the station can keep the towns economy running, even when there aren’t that many trains coming in Break road trip shots Script: Heading to the Eastern Cape we follow a former district line , from Gquberha to Graaf Reniet, once a major freight route cut off 30 years ago. Surprisingly Transnet appeared to be reviving this branch investing millions repairing the line. Johan There was a bridge here where you could walk to the station, and there was a platform, a neat platform, there were fish ponds here. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Abandoned railway towns tell the story of colonial and economic conquest, and the failure to embrace and maintain vital transport routes.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The South African rail network is an historical map of colonial conquest. In the late 1800s, as mining developed in the interior, rail lines were built connecting the mines to the ports, and steam trains criss-crossed the vast South Africa landscape. They played a vital role in the South African (Anglo-Boer) War, and bridges built in the 1800s are still standing. By 1912 when the Union Government was formed, the four rail networks were amalgamated and taken over by the government, becoming a powerful economic and political tool. In 1924 after the industrial Depression, the white – “European” - minority enjoyed the first affirmative action appointments - unskilled white labour was actively recruited onto the railways to ensure they did not sink below the level of the “non-European” workers, and black rail employee numbers were eclipsed by white workers. Entire towns were developed around the railways, providing a vast network of solidly built brick houses and recreational facilities for white employees, with crude rondavels provided for migrant black workers. The South African Railways and Harbours, SAR&H, ran these towns, with the station masters playing the role of mayor, and the railway police keeping people in their place. The SAR&H built tracks deep into the farming areas, providing sidings for farmers to leave their milk for collection, collect their post, and deliver their produce to market. It ensured political patronage, but over time this vast network became uneconomical. Coal was cheap, and with a ready supply of white artisans and labour, South Africa kept steam trains running for far longer than the rest of the world. But when railway workers’ kids left and got University degrees, the white train drivers refused to have black stokers and train assistants in their cabs, Steam began to die and diesel engines took over. The uneconomical routes were gradually abandoned and entire towns began to die - Klipplaat and Touws River are prime examples, both were substantial depots and railway towns in their heyday. Today they are sad, falling-apart towns, the majority of adult residents dependent on SASSA grants, with the few available jobs provided by the municipality and surrounding farms.
metadata.Summary: Every station and rail siding leading to these towns has been abandoned, vandalised, and scrap dealers have fed off them like vultures. This vast infrastructure and state asset was simply abandoned as senior Transnet officials began to run and own lucrative trucking companies. Indecision and lack of leadership in the protection of assets has resulted in every railway station either destroyed or occupied by farm workers. Transnet’s lack of vision or any clear policy of transferring ownership has resulted in buildings either being burnt for insurance claims or simply destroyed as an act of defiance. Today people in these forgotten towns equate the failed Transnet with the failures of the ANC, and the overloaded, crumbling highways are dominated by lucrative trucking companies, often owned by politicians. But in fact, the railways began to fade and abandon both their employees and their infrastructure in the mid-1980s under the Nationalist Government. We will tell this history through two towns. Klipplaat and Touws River, with two main characters in each town. Willie Marais was a stream train driver born directly opposite the station in Touws River, which was built in 1881. His father was a “poor white” who never managed to own his own home. Willie grew up with the benefits of a good high school, now vandalised and abandoned, and recreational facilities provided for the white workers, with movies on Saturday night in the railway hall, and security ensured by the railway police. In 1992 he was retrenched. He spent the next 20 years working as an undertaker across the country. He has returned to Touws River to restore the home he grew up in, with dreams of also restoring the demolished station to its former glory. It was burnt for an alleged insurance payout, and taken apart brick by brick, one roof sheet at a time. Willie manged to save two of the verandah pillars which were built from ships’ masts in the 1800s. Louis Langeveld is an elder of Klipplaat, now retired. He was the headmaster of Klipplaat High. His father worked for the railways and his childhood is richly populated with memories of a thriving railway town. His father witnessed the royal visit of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth together with their daughters Elizabeth and Margaret in 1947 when the train stopped in Klipplaat to take on coal and water. The station master hosted them for a meal at the station in its once-grand wooded dining hall. Louis used to fetch the Saturday night films from the train and snuck into the projection room, hiding from the station master and his railway police lackeys – he was not allowed in the hall as he is coloured. In 1986 when economic sanctions began to bite, SAR&H employees were offered retrenchment packages or transfers to bigger depots. The town’s demographic in 1986 was 2,500 whites, 2,000 coloured inhabitants and roughly 1,000 black Africans. Today only two white people remain, Johan and his wife Chantel Loggerenberg, they own and run the former Railway Hotel, now the Hotel Charles, and the rest of the population of 13,000 are either living in shacks or in the railway houses. Johan van Loggerenberg is a secondary character in the Klipplaat story. He was born in Klipplaat, and went to the junior schools and the middle school in town. He lived in one of the “white” railway houses built in the 1940s. His father worked as a rail assistant until he was retrenched. As the railway workers left one by one, the shops began to close and slowly the coloured people began to buy up the old railway houses built for the whites. Now the four taverns and three shops are owned by Ethiopian and Somalian shopkeepers. People survive off SASSA grants and the few jobs provided by the Municipality.
metadata.Further information: The people of Klipplaat are bitter about being abandoned by Transnet and every SAR&H building that was not occupied has been systematically destroyed. The only remnant of the heyday of this railway town is a sad, heavily graffitied steam engine. Enroute to Gqeberha, there are many abandoned sidings - Mount Stewart has the most beautiful old Methodist church, and a trading store built by the Cawood clan. Rich in settler history, the Cawood clan farmed here for generations and the trading store still operated until a few years back. Today, Richelle and David Olifant live in the station master’s house. They are farm workers, and remember trains passing in 2018. At Baroe siding, the station houses are inhabited by Shane Martins and Joane van Wyk. Three years and one month ago they visited the Transnet offices in Uitenhage to get permission to live in the houses - they are still waiting for the contract. They moved here off the farms to be closer to transport. In 2020 the last train went past carrying stones from a quarry down the line to Gqeberha.
